paragraphs.heading: Two dead stars collide
paragraphs.text: A neutron star merger is a collision between two neutron stars. Once two of them orbit each other, they lose energy as gravitational radiation and slowly spiral closer together. When they finally meet, they form either a heavier neutron star or, if the leftover mass is above the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit, a black hole.

paragraphs.heading: Flashes and glows
paragraphs.text: The merger can build a magnetic field trillions of times stronger than Earth's in just a millisecond or two. It sets off a short gamma-ray burst that can be seen across hundreds of millions or even billions of light-years. It also makes a kilonova: a short-lived glow of longer-wave light shining in all directions, powered by the radioactive decay of heavy nuclei made and flung out in the crash.

paragraphs.heading: Forging heavy elements
paragraphs.text: For a brief moment the merger floods its surroundings with so many neutrons that the r-process can take place. This reaction is responsible for making about half of the isotopes of elements heavier than iron. Kilonovae had been discussed as a home for the r-process since 1998, but the idea only became widely accepted after an event called GW170817 was seen in 2017.

paragraphs.heading: The 2017 event
paragraphs.text: On 17 August 2017 the LIGO and Virgo detectors picked up GW170817, gravitational waves from two neutron stars merging in the galaxy NGC 4993, about 140 million light-years away in the constellation Hydra. Just 1.7 seconds after the wave signal, a short gamma-ray burst lasting roughly 2 seconds was detected, and 11 hours later a source of visible light was spotted. The burst matched the waves in both place and time, which settled that these mergers make short gamma-ray bursts. The visible light appeared where the other two signals came from and looked just as a kilonova should, showing that mergers make kilonovae as well.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the universe
paragraphs.text: Scientists have also shown a new way to use gravitational waves, especially from neutron star mergers, to find the Hubble constant, which sets how fast the universe expands. The two older methods, one based on redshifts and one on the cosmic distance ladder, disagree by about 10%. That gap is called the Hubble tension, and using kilonovae as another kind of standard candle might help settle it.

paragraphs.heading: More mergers
paragraphs.text: In April 2019 LIGO and Virgo announced GW190425, an event with a 99.94% chance of being two neutron stars merging. Even after a wide follow-up search, no light from it could be found. In 2019 too, data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory revealed another such merger 6.6 billion light-years away, seen as an X-ray signal called XT2. That merger left behind a magnetar, whose emissions could be followed for several hours.

paragraphs.heading: A danger to life on Earth
paragraphs.text: These mergers give off an unusually varied mix of radiation that could harm life on Earth. The harmless gravitational waves arrive first, the gamma rays and afterglow follow seconds to hours later, and cosmic rays come hundreds to thousands of years after that. Any merger within 10 parsecs of Earth would end humanity, and so would a direct hit from the tightly aimed gamma-ray beam. But such mergers are thought to be much rarer than supernovae, and the beam would have to point exactly at Earth, so the overall threat is extremely low.
